newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: "Experimental" trade in African ivory recommended.
newsitem.headline: "Experimental" trade in African ivory recommended.

text.p: A committee at a world forum on endangered species recommended on Thursday that three southern African states be allowed to sell ivory to Japan in 18 months on an experimental basis and under strict monitoring.

The 19-member committee -- set up on Wednesday by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) to try to find a compromise to a controversial proposal by Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia to be exempted from a 1989 world ban in ivory trade -- also recommended these countries' elephant herds be transferred to a tradeable species list from the no-trade one.
In a draft amendment that will be debated by the 138-member CITES on Thursday, the committee however said the transfer to this list, called Appendix II, does not include automatic trade.

"The transfer would include no international trade before 18 months after the transfer to Appendix II comes into effect. Thereafter an experimental quota of raw ivory may be traded with Japan," the draft says.
Botswana would be entitled to sell 25.3 tonnes of raw ivory, Zimbabwe 20 tonnes and Namibia 13.8 tonnes "under an international reporting and monitoring system", it says.

The three countries are demanding trade, arguing that their combined elephant herd of about 150,000, has been growing steadily and was doing so even before the world banned trade in ivory to protect elephants from extinction.

The 10-day CITES conference postponed for the second time in 24 hours voting on the proposal by Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia, saying many delegates had indicated in overnight consultations they wanted the issue to be thoroughly thrashed by a special working group.
CITES first postponed a vote on the issue on Tuesday after a four-hour debate that went well past the conference closing time.
The ivory trade and African elephant debate has overshadowed all other issues at the CITES meeting which ends on Friday.
Zimbabwe's Environment and Tourism Minister Chen Chimutengwende said a possible compromise could be worked around an amendment proposed by South Africa but was defeated by a slim margin on Tuesday.
"There is room to work around that," he told Reuters.

South Africa's proposed amendment to ease the ban to allow commercial trade to start only in 1999, with some fixed quotas, was just three votes short of the 78 three-thirds majority it needed from the 123 countries that voted. Forty-one countries voted against the amendment, and seven abstained.

The ivory trade proposal is strongly backed by Japan and Switzerland but has faced stiff opposition from influential green movements and countries, including the United States and from the European Union, who argue that easing the ban will leave elephants at the mercy of poachers.
The special CITES committee said trade should only be allowed when the convention was satisfied with the monitoring measures proposed by Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia and Japan.
